column1: #   expectation: valid       pyHanko opens the file and judges the signature VALID
#                invalid     pyHanko opens the file and judges the signature INVALID
#                unreadable  pyHanko refuses the file before reaching the signature
# A file may appear more than once, under different trust modes: that is how the
# rotation rows prove each artifact verifies against its own key and not the other.

column4: PAdES B-B, sealed by the fixture leaf under the fixture root.
Page geometry changed inside the signed byte range, same file length.
The /ByteRange claims past the end of a file that still parses, so the coverage rule is what refuses it.
Tail removed with the trailer, so the file cannot be opened at all.
An unexpected revision appended, redefining the page object.
The CMS of another sealed document spliced into /Contents.
Cryptographically sound but sealed with a key outside the trusted root.
The executed agreement produced by the staged finalization: reviewed revision, field values, appended completion report, sealed at PAdES B-B under the fixture root.
Sealed under the RETIRED key (fixture-seal-2026-a), validated against the retired certificate's own anchor. A rotation does not invalidate what the old key sealed.
Sealed under the ACTIVE key after rotation (fixture-seal-2026-b), validated against the new certificate's anchor.
The retired artifact under the NEW key's anchor: refused. The two anchors discriminate, so the VALID verdicts above are about the right certificate and not about a validator that trusts everything.
The active artifact under the RETIRED key's anchor: refused. The complement of the row above.
PAdES B-T. The TSA certificate chains to a publicly trusted root, so the timestamp is trusted as well as sound.
PAdES B-T with a cryptographically sound timestamp from an authority whose root is trusted nowhere: judged invalid on TSA trust alone.
